pos: n. (a cutting tool; rendering Hebrew garzen, Greek axine)
etymology: Old English aex. Scripture uses the axe for felling, for judgment, and once for a famous miracle of recovery.
biblical_def: An axe fells timber. Isaiah uses it to rebuke a boasting empire: “Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?” (Isa 10:15) — the instrument taking credit for the arm. John the Baptist announces judgment with it: “now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees” (Mat 3:10). And Elisha makes iron swim when a borrowed axe head falls into Jordan (2Ki 6:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines axe as an instrument for hewing timber and chopping wood, consisting of an iron blade with a steel edge fixed to a helve or handle.
webster_full: AX, n. An instrument for hewing timber and chopping wood, consisting of an iron blade or head with a steel edge fixed to a helve or handle.
scriptures: Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood.
Mat 3:10
And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.
But as one was felling a beam, the axe head fell into the water: and he cried, and said, Alas, master! for it was borrowed. axe
Deu 19:5

As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live:
corruption_summary: Gifted people routinely mistake themselves for the reason things happen, which is exactly the boast Isaiah puts in the mouth of a tool.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's mockery works because the absurdity is obvious in the object and invisible in the man: shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? Assyria was a real instrument doing real damage, and God names it as the rod of His anger — which is precisely why its self-congratulation was ridiculous. Effectiveness is not evidence of independence.

Elisha's miracle carries a small pastoral kindness. The axe head was borrowed, and the young prophet's distress was over another man's property. God's power was spent on a debt an ordinary man could not repay, which is a very small matter to trouble heaven with and evidently not too small.
roots_summary: Hebrew garzen (H1631), an axe; Greek axine (G513), an axe — used only of John's warning.
roots_lines: Hebrew garzen (H1631) — axe; Deuteronomy 19:5, Isaiah 10:15.
Greek axine (G513) — axe; Matthew 3:10, Luke 3:9, laid unto the root of the trees.
usage: “Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?” — the tool taking credit.
“The axe is laid unto the root of the trees” — judgment at the root, not the branches.
“Alas, master! for it was borrowed” — a small debt worth troubling heaven with.

pos: n. (a rounded vessel; rendering Hebrew gullah and mizraq)
etymology: Old English bolla. Scripture's bowls hold oil for lamps, blood for altars, and wine for the careless.
biblical_def: A bowl is a rounded vessel. Zechariah's vision sets one above a candlestick, feeding seven lamps by seven pipes (Zec 4:2) — a picture of supply the lamps do not generate. Ecclesiastes uses a breaking bowl for death: “or the golden bowl be broken” (Ecc 12:6). Gideon wrings a bowlful of dew from the fleece (Jdg 6:38), and Amos condemns those that “drink wine in bowls” while the nation falls (Amo 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bowl as a concave vessel to hold liquors, rather wide than deep; and the hollow part of any thing.
webster_full: BOWL, n. A concave vessel to hold liquors, rather wide than deep, in distinction from a cup, which is rather deep than wide.
2. The hollow part of any thing.
scriptures: Zec 4:2

And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof:
Ecc 12:6
Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.
Jdg 6:38
And it was so: for he rose up early on the morrow, and thrust the fleece together, and wringed the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.
Amo 6:6
That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.
corruption_summary: Ministries work at producing light and neglect the supply that feeds it, which is precisely the arrangement Zechariah's vision was given to correct.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah's candlestick has a detail the tabernacle's lacked: a bowl on top with pipes running to each lamp. The lamps burn but do not manufacture; the oil comes from above and outside. When Zechariah asks what it means, the answer is the verse everyone quotes without its picture — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. The vision is a plumbing diagram for ministry.
roots_summary: Hebrew gullah (H1543), a rounded bowl or oil reservoir; mizraq (H4219), a sprinkling bowl of the altar service.
roots_lines: Hebrew gullah (H1543) — bowl, reservoir; Zechariah 4:2-3, Ecclesiastes 12:6.
Hebrew mizraq (H4219) — basin, bowl; Amos 6:6, Numbers 7:13, the offerings of the princes.
usage: “A candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it” — supply from above the lamps.
“Or the golden bowl be broken” — Ecclesiastes on the end of life.
“That drink wine in bowls” — comfort while the nation falls.

etymology: Old English sceath, a covering. A sheath is where a sword waits — and Scripture's drama is usually in the drawing or the returning.
biblical_def: A sheath holds a sword. David takes Goliath's sword “out of the sheath thereof” to finish him (1Sa 17:51). Ezekiel announces judgment as a drawing that will not reverse: “I will draw forth my sword out of his sheath” (Eze 21:3). And Christ commands the opposite motion in Gethsemane: “Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?” (Joh 18:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sheath as a case for the reception of a sword or other long instrument; a scabbard.
webster_full: SHEATH, n. A case for the reception of a sword or other long and slender instrument; a scabbard.
2. Any thin defensive covering.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto Peter, Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?

Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.
Eze 21:3
And say to the land of Israel, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I am against thee, and will draw forth my sword out of his sheath, and will cut off from thee the righteous and the wicked.
And the LORD commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof.
corruption_summary: Zeal reaches for a weapon at the moment of crisis, and Christ's word to the most loyal man present was to put it away.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's swing in the garden was brave, loyal, and entirely wrong, and Christ's rebuke supplies the reason: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it? A sword drawn to prevent the cross would have prevented salvation. There are moments when defending Christ means obstructing Him, and the disciple most willing to fight is the one most likely to reach that point without noticing.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadan (H5084), a sheath; taar (H8593), a scabbard or razor-case; Greek theke (G2336), a receptacle.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadan (H5084) — sheath; 1 Chronicles 21:27, the angel put up his sword again.
Greek theke (G2336) — sheath, case; only John 18:11, put up thy sword into the sheath.
usage: “Put up thy sword into the sheath” — loyalty told to stand down.
“I will draw forth my sword out of his sheath” — a drawing that will not reverse.
“He put it up again into the sheath thereof” — judgment stayed at the threshingfloor.

pos: n. pl. (sounding ornaments; rendering Hebrew paamon and metsillah)
etymology: Old English belle. The high priest's bells were sewn to his hem so the congregation could hear him working where they could not see.
biblical_def: Bells are sounding ornaments. Golden bells alternated with pomegranates on the hem of the priest's robe, “and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD, and when he cometh out, that he die not” (Exo 28:35). Zechariah's last vision promises that ordinary things will bear sanctuary holiness: “In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” (Zec 14:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bell as a vessel or hollow body, used for making sounds, cast of a composition of copper and tin.
webster_full: BELL, n. A vessel or hollow body, used for making sounds. Its constituent parts are a barrel or hollow body, the clapper within, and the ear or cannon by which it is hung.
2. A hollow body of metal, perforated, and containing a solid ball, to give sounds.
scriptures: And beneath upon the hem of it thou shalt make pomegranates of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, round about the hem thereof; and bells of gold between them round about:
And it shall be upon Aaron to minister: and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD, and when he cometh out, that he die not.
In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the LORD'S house shall be like the bowls before the altar.
And they made bells of pure gold, and put the bells between the pomegranates upon the hem of the robe, round about between the pomegranates;
corruption_summary: Christ's present intercession is invisible and therefore easily forgotten, and the bells existed precisely so an unseeing congregation could know the priest was still at work.
corruption_paragraphs: The bells solved a pastoral problem. Israel could not follow the high priest past the veil, so a sound moving along the hem told them he was alive and serving on their behalf. Hebrews makes the application without needing the image: he ever liveth to make intercession for them. A believer who cannot see his Advocate is in exactly the position of the congregation outside — and Zechariah's promise, that even horse-bells will be inscribed HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD, says where all of this is going.
roots_summary: Hebrew paamon (H6472), a bell of the priestly robe; metsillah (H4698), a jingling bell, in Zechariah 14:20.
roots_lines: Hebrew paamon (H6472) — bell; Exodus 28:33-34, 39:25-26, on the hem of the robe.
Hebrew metsillah (H4698) — bell; only Zechariah 14:20, the bells of the horses.
usage: “His sound shall be heard when he goeth in… and when he cometh out” — proof of a working priest.
“A golden bell and a pomegranate” — sound and fruit alternating on the hem.
“Upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” — the ordinary made sacred.

etymology: From Old French baril. The Hebrew is a large earthen jar — the KJV's barrel is a household meal-vessel, not a cask.
biblical_def: A barrel is a large jar. The widow of Zarephath has “an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse” (1Ki 17:12), and the promise attached is one of continuance rather than abundance: “The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail” (1Ki 17:14) — and it did not, though it never filled either. Elijah later has four barrels of water poured on the Carmel altar three times (1Ki 18:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines barrel as a vessel of more length than breadth, round and bulging in the middle, made of staves and heading, and bound with hoops.
webster_full: BARREL, n. A vessel or cask, of more length than breadth, round and bulging in the middle, made of staves and heading, and bound with hoops.
2. The quantity which a barrel contains.
3. Any thing long and hollow; as the barrel of a gun.
scriptures: And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.
For thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.
And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.
And he put the wood in order, and cut the bullock in pieces, and laid him on the wood, and said, Fill four barrels with water, and pour it on the burnt sacrifice, and on the wood.
corruption_summary: Believers pray for the barrel to be filled, when the promise given at Zarephath was that it would not empty — daily sufficiency rather than visible security.
corruption_paragraphs: The miracle at Zarephath is easy to misremember as abundance. The text says otherwise: the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD. Every morning there was a handful, and every morning it was enough, and at no point could the widow have looked in the jar and felt secure. That is the shape of most provision in Scripture — manna that could not be stored, bread asked for daily — and it keeps faith current rather than retired.
roots_summary: Hebrew kad (H3537), a jar or pitcher — the same vessel Rebekah carried and Gideon's men broke.
roots_lines: Hebrew kad (H3537) — jar, barrel, pitcher; 1 Kings 17:12-16, 18:33, Genesis 24:14, Judges 7:16.
Hebrew qemach (H7058) — meal, flour; the handful that did not waste.
usage: “An handful of meal in a barrel” — the whole estate of a widow.
“The barrel of meal shall not waste” — continuance, not abundance.
“Fill four barrels with water” — Carmel's deliberate handicap.

pos: n. (the upper edge of a vessel or bank; rendering Hebrew saphah, Greek ano)
etymology: Middle English brimme, an edge. The brim is the limit of what a vessel will hold — and Scripture twice makes a point of filling to it.
biblical_def: A brim is an upper edge. Jordan “overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest” when the priests' feet dip in the brim of the water and it parts (Jos 3:15). At Cana Christ says, “Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim” (Joh 2:7). The molten sea in Solomon's temple had a brim “wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies” (1Ki 7:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brim as the rim, lip or broad border of any vessel or other thing; and the upper edge of the bank of a fountain, river or other body of water.
webster_full: BRIM, n. The rim, lip or broad border of any vessel or other thing.
2. The upper edge of the bank of a fountain, river, or other body of water; the margin or shore.
scriptures: Joh 2:7
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
Jos 3:15

And as they that bare the ark were come unto Jordan, and the feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water, (for Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest,)
And it was an hand breadth thick, and the brim thereof was wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies: it contained two thousand baths.
Joh 2:9
When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
corruption_summary: Obedience is usually rendered to the minimum that satisfies the instruction, and at Cana the servants filled the jars to the brim when half would have looked obedient.
corruption_paragraphs: John records the detail deliberately: they filled them up to the brim. Six stone waterpots, twenty or thirty gallons apiece, drawn and carried by hand for a wedding that had already run out. Nobody would have known if they had been three-quarters full, and the miracle would have worked either way — but the quantity of wine produced was determined by how far the servants obeyed. Christ turned what was given, and they gave the maximum the vessels would take.
roots_summary: Hebrew saphah (H8193), lip, edge, brim — the same word for the lip of a person and the brim of a vessel; Greek ano (G507), to the top.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphah (H8193) — lip, edge, brim; Joshua 3:15, 1 Kings 7:26, Exodus 28:32.
Greek heos ano (G2193/G507) — up to the top; John 2:7, they filled them up to the brim.
usage: “They filled them up to the brim” — the yield followed the filling.
“The feet of the priests… were dipped in the brim of the water” — Jordan at flood.
“Wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies” — the molten sea.

etymology: Middle English busch. One bush in Scripture outranks every other — a thornbush in Midian that burned without being consumed.
biblical_def: A bush is a shrub. The definitive one is at Horeb: “the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2). Moses turns aside to see “this great sight” (Exo 3:3), and the episode becomes shorthand for the whole revelation — Christ cites “the place concerning the bush” as proof of resurrection (Mar 12:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bush as a thick shrub; also a cluster of shrubs; and a shrub with branches, cut off and set at the door of a tavern.
webster_full: BUSH, n. A thick shrub; also, a cluster of shrubs.
2. An assemblage of thick branches of trees.
3. A branch of a tree fixed or hung out as a tavern sign.
scriptures: Exo 3:2
And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
Exo 3:3
And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?

And for the precious things of the earth and fulness thereof, and for the good will of him that dwelt in the bush: let the blessing come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the top of the head of him that was separated from his brethren.
corruption_summary: Encounters with God are expected in impressive settings, and the definitive one occurred in a desert weed that anyone else would have walked past.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew seneh is a thornbush — scrub, not cedar. God chose the least significant vegetation in the wilderness and made it the place where He named Himself I AM. Moses' part was simply that he turned aside to see; the sight had presumably been visible for some minutes to a man who was watching sheep. Attention was the whole qualification. Christ later called the passage the place concerning the bush and used it to prove the resurrection, since God said I am — not I was — the God of Abraham.
roots_summary: Hebrew seneh (H5572), a thornbush — possibly the root behind Sinai; Greek batos (G942), a bramble.
roots_lines: Hebrew seneh (H5572) — thornbush; Exodus 3:2-4, Deuteronomy 33:16, him that dwelt in the bush.
Greek batos (G942) — bramble bush; Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37, Acts 7:30, 35.
usage: “The bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” — the sight that stopped Moses.
“I will now turn aside, and see this great sight” — attention was the qualification.
“In the bush God spake unto him” — Christ's proof of the resurrection.

pos: n. (a bunch of grapes; rendering Hebrew eshkol)
etymology: Old English clyster. In Scripture the cluster is almost always of grapes, and almost always evidence about a land.
biblical_def: A cluster is a bunch of fruit. The spies cut one at Eshcol so large that they “bare it between two upon a staff” (Num 13:23) — proof the land was good, carried by men who then advised against entering it. The bride calls her beloved “a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi” (Son 1:14). Moses' song calls the enemy's grapes “grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter” (Deu 32:32), and Revelation gathers “the clusters of the vine of the earth” for the winepress (Rev 14:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cluster as a bunch; a number of things of the same kind growing or joined together; a knot.
webster_full: CLUSTER, n. A bunch; a number of things of the same kind growing or joined together; a knot; as a cluster of raisins.
2. A number of individuals or things collected or gathered into a close body.
scriptures: And they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff; and they brought of the pomegranates, and of the figs.
Son 1:14
My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi.
For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: of the

And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.
corruption_summary: Evidence rarely settles a fear, and the spies carried the proof of God's goodness on a pole while arguing that the land could not be taken.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 13 is a study in what evidence cannot do. Ten men carried a single cluster of grapes so heavy it needed two men and a staff, laid it before the congregation, said surely it floweth with milk and honey, and then said nevertheless the people be strong. The fruit did not change a single mind, including their own. Unbelief is not a shortage of data; Caleb saw the same grapes and the same giants and reached the opposite conclusion because he was reckoning with a different factor.
roots_summary: Hebrew eshkol (H811), a cluster — also the name of the valley where the spies cut it; Greek botrus (G1009), a cluster of grapes.
roots_lines: Hebrew eshkol (H811) — cluster; Numbers 13:23-24, the brook Eshcol, named for the cluster.
Greek botrus (G1009) — cluster of grapes; only Revelation 14:18.
usage: “They bare it between two upon a staff” — proof that changed nobody's mind.
“A cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi” — the bride's praise.
“Gather the clusters of the vine of the earth” — the harvest of wrath.

pos: n., v. (a winnowing shovel; rendering Hebrew mizreh, Greek ptuon)
etymology: From Latin vannus, a winnowing basket. The biblical fan is not for cooling but for throwing threshed grain into the wind.
biblical_def: A fan winnows. John the Baptist describes the Coming One with it: “whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Mat 3:12). Isaiah promises Israel will fan her enemies away (Isa 41:16), and Jeremiah warns, “I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land” (Jer 15:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fan as an instrument used by ladies to move the air and cool the face; and an instrument for winnowing grain, by moving the air.
webster_full: FAN, n. An instrument used by ladies to move the air and cool the face.
2. An instrument for winnowing grain, by moving the air.
FAN, v.t. To winnow; to ventilate; to separate the chaff from the grain and blow it away.
scriptures: Mat 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Jer 15:7
And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways.
Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel.
Luk 3:17
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.
corruption_summary: Separation is expected at the end of the world and nowhere else, when John says the fan is already in His hand and the floor is being purged now.
corruption_paragraphs: Winnowing is a violent, patient business: the threshed heap is thrown into the air repeatedly so the wind carries off what has no weight. John's picture assumes wheat and chaff currently lie on the same floor, indistinguishable to anyone standing on it, and that the sorting is done by throwing everything up. That is a fair description of how trials operate in a congregation — and the promise attached is that the wheat goes into the garner, gathered rather than scattered.
roots_summary: Hebrew mizreh (H4214), a winnowing fork; zarah (H2219), to scatter or winnow; Greek ptuon (G4425), a winnowing shovel.
roots_lines: Hebrew mizreh (H4214) — winnowing fan; Isaiah 30:24, Jeremiah 15:7.
Greek ptuon (G4425) — winnowing shovel; Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17, whose fan is in his hand.
usage: “Whose fan is in his hand” — the sorting already begun.
“He will throughly purge his floor” — nothing left half-sorted.
“I will fan them with a fan in the gates” — Jeremiah's judgment.

etymology: Old English cnif. The Hebrew word for the knife Abraham carried is built on the root for eating — a sacrificial blade.
biblical_def: A knife cuts. The heaviest in Scripture is Abraham's: “Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son” (Gen 22:10), stopped mid-motion by the angel. Joshua makes sharp knives to circumcise Israel at Gilgal (Jos 5:2). Proverbs advises a knife at one's own throat against appetite (Pro 23:2), and Jeremiah's scroll is cut with a penknife and burned by a king (Jer 36:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knife as a cutting instrument with a sharp edge; and a sword or dagger.
webster_full: KNIFE, n. A cutting instrument with a sharp edge.
2. A sword or dagger.
scriptures: And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.
Jos 5:2
At that time the LORD said unto Joshua, Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time.
Pro 23:2
And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
corruption_summary: Genesis 22 is read as a story about Abraham's obedience, and it is — but it is chiefly a story about a Father who did not withhold His Son when no angel called.
corruption_paragraphs: The knife is the point at which Genesis 22 becomes unbearable and then becomes gospel. Abraham stretched forth his hand and took the knife; the arm was raised, the intention complete, and only then did the voice come. A ram was caught in a thicket and a son walked down the mountain. Centuries later, on ground the chapter names Jehovah-jireh, another Father brought a Son to a hill and no voice interrupted, because the substitute this time was the Son Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew maakeleth (H3979), a large knife, from akal, to eat; taar (H8593), a penknife or razor, in Jeremiah 36:23.
roots_lines: Hebrew maakeleth (H3979) — slaughter knife; Genesis 22:6, 10, Judges 19:29.
Hebrew tsor (H6864) — flint; Joshua 5:2, make thee sharp knives.
usage: “Took the knife to slay his son” — the arm raised before the voice came.
“Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again” — the covenant renewed at Gilgal.
“Cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire” — a king editing Scripture.

etymology: Old English naegel. Scripture's nails fasten tent pegs, temple doors, wise words, and one crucified Body.
biblical_def: Nails fasten. Jael drives a tent nail through Sisera's temples (Jdg 4:21). Ecclesiastes commends words of the wise as “nails fastened by the masters of assemblies” (Ecc 12:11). Isaiah promises Eliakim will be “a nail in a sure place” (Isa 22:23), and Thomas names the evidence he requires: “except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails… I will not believe” (Joh 20:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nail as the claw or talon of a fowl or beast; the horny substance at the end of the human fingers; and a small pointed piece of metal, to be driven into a board or other piece of timber.
webster_full: NAIL, n. The claw or talon of a fowl or beast.
2. The horny substance growing at the end of the human fingers and toes.
3. A small pointed piece of metal, usually with a head, to be driven into a board or other piece of timber, to fasten it to other timber.
scriptures: The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house.

The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
Jdg 4:21

Then Jael Heber's wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died. and
corruption_summary: Teaching aims to be memorable rather than fixed, and Ecclesiastes commends the opposite — words driven in like nails, uncomfortable and immovable.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 12:11 gives preaching two images at once: the words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies. A goad prods a reluctant animal forward; a nail holds something in place permanently. Good teaching does both — it moves people who do not want to move, and it fixes truth where it cannot drift. Neither image is comfortable, and both assume the hearer would otherwise wander or come loose.

Thomas asked for the nail prints and was given them, along with a rebuke that is also a blessing for everyone since: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed. The marks were kept in a resurrection body, which means the risen Christ carries the evidence of His own execution permanently.
roots_summary: Hebrew masmer (H4548), a nail or spike; yathed (H3489), a tent peg — Jael's weapon and Isaiah's sure place; Greek helos (G2247), a nail.
roots_lines: Hebrew yathed (H3489) — peg, nail; Judges 4:21, Isaiah 22:23, a nail in a sure place.
Greek helos (G2247) — nail; only John 20:25, the print of the nails.
usage: “As nails fastened by the masters of assemblies” — teaching that holds.
“I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place” — Eliakim's commission.
“The print of the nails” — evidence kept in a resurrection body.

pos: n. pl. (heavy cords; rendering Hebrew abothah, Greek schoinion)
etymology: Old English rap. Ropes in Scripture bind prisoners, signal surrender, and are once cut loose in a storm as an act of faith.
biblical_def: Ropes are heavy cords. Delilah binds Samson with new ropes, which he breaks “from off his arms like a thread” (Jdg 16:12). Ben-hadad's servants put ropes on their heads as a sign of surrender to Ahab (1Ki 20:31). In Paul's shipwreck the soldiers “cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off” (Act 27:32) — destroying the only escape so that all would stay with the ship, as Paul had said they must.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rope as a large string or line composed of several strands twisted together; and any collection of things united in a string.
webster_full: ROPE, n. A large string or line composed of several strands twisted together.
2. A row or string consisting of a number of things united; as a rope of onions.
scriptures: Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off.

Delilah therefore took new ropes, and bound him therewith, and said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And there were liers in wait abiding in the chamber. And he brake them from off his arms like a thread.

And his servants said unto him, Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings: let us, I pray thee, put sackcloth on our loins, and ropes upon our heads, and go out to the king of Israel: peradventure he will save thy life.
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
corruption_summary: Faith is usually asked to add something; at Acts 27 it required cutting away the lifeboat, so that trusting the promise became the only remaining option.
corruption_paragraphs: The sailors had lowered the boat under pretence of laying out anchors, intending to escape and leave the passengers. Paul saw it and told the centurion, except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and the soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat fall away. God had promised every life; the promise did not remove the requirement to stay aboard. Sometimes obedience means destroying the alternative that would have made faith unnecessary.
roots_summary: Hebrew abothah (H5688), a twisted cord or rope; chebel (H2256), a cord or line; Greek schoinion (G4979), a rope of rushes.
roots_lines: Hebrew abothah (H5688) — rope, cord; Judges 16:11-12, new ropes that never occupied.
Greek schoinion (G4979) — rope, cord; Acts 27:32, and John 2:15, a scourge of small cords.
usage: “Cut off the ropes of the boat, and let her fall off” — the escape destroyed.
“Brake them from off his arms like a thread” — Samson's strength before it left.
“Put ropes upon our heads” — the posture of surrender.

pos: n. (a piece of wood; rendering Hebrew ets, Greek phruganon)
etymology: Old English sticca. A stick is the plainest object in Scripture, and it is repeatedly the material of a sign.
biblical_def: A stick is a piece of wood. Ezekiel is told to take two and join them: “join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand” (Eze 37:17), a sign of Judah and Israel reunited. The widow of Zarephath is gathering two sticks to cook a last meal (1Ki 17:10). Paul gathers a bundle of sticks on Malta and is bitten by a viper out of the heat (Act 28:3), and a man is stoned for gathering them on the sabbath (Num 15:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stick as the small shoot or branch of a tree or shrub, cut off; a rod; and a staff.
webster_full: STICK, n. The small shoot or branch of a tree or shrub, cut off; a rod; also, a staff.
2. Any stem of a plant of a size to be cut for fuel.
scriptures: And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand.

So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, the widow woman was there gathering of sticks: and he called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.
Act 28:3
And when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks, and laid them on the fire, there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.
And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day.
corruption_summary: Unity is pursued by argument and negotiation, and Ezekiel's sign shows two sticks becoming one in the prophet's hand — the joining done by someone other than the sticks.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 37's second sign follows the valley of dry bones and belongs with it. Two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, are written on and then joined so that they become one in thine hand. The prophet does the joining; the sticks contribute nothing but their separateness. Set beside the bones that could not assemble themselves, the message is consistent — both resurrection and reunion are acts of God, and the people involved are told to prophesy rather than to organize.
roots_summary: Hebrew ets (H6086), wood or tree — the same word for a living tree and a cut stick; Greek phruganon (G5434), dry sticks or brushwood.
roots_lines: Hebrew ets (H6086) — tree, wood, stick; Ezekiel 37:16-20, 1 Kings 17:10.
Greek phruganon (G5434) — dry sticks, brushwood; only Acts 28:3, Paul's bundle on Malta.
usage: “They shall become one in thine hand” — the joining is not the sticks' work.
“Gathering of two sticks” — the widow's last meal.
“Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks” — the apostle doing the fire duty.

pos: n. (an instrument of work; rendering Hebrew chereb and cheret)
etymology: Old English tol. Scripture's most striking instruction about tools is a prohibition — where they may not be used.
biblical_def: A tool is a working instrument. The law forbids one on the altar: “if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone: for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it” (Exo 20:25). Solomon's temple was built so that “there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building” (1Ki 6:7). Aaron shapes the golden calf “with a graving tool” (Exo 32:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tool as an instrument of manual operation, particularly such as are used by farmers and mechanics; and a person used as an instrument by another.
webster_full: TOOL, n. An instrument of manual operation, particularly such as are used by farmers and mechanics.
2. A person used as an instrument by another person; a word of reproach.
scriptures: And if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone: for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it.

And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.
Exo 32:4

And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Deu 27:5
And there shalt thou build an altar unto the LORD thy God, an altar of stones: thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them.
corruption_summary: Worship is improved with technique until the improvement becomes the thing offered, which is the exact reasoning the altar law was given to forbid.
corruption_paragraphs: The altar prohibition is counterintuitive: God asks for uncut stone and says that lifting a tool upon it pollutes it. Skill is not condemned elsewhere — the tabernacle required extraordinary craftsmanship, Spirit-given — but at the altar, the place of atonement, human improvement is excluded entirely. Nothing of ours is to be added to the place where our sin is dealt with. The calf, by contrast, was made with a graving tool, and it was the one thing at Sinai that human skill produced entirely on its own initiative.
roots_summary: Hebrew chereb (H2719), a cutting instrument or sword — the word in Exodus 20:25; cheret (H2747), a graving tool.
roots_lines: Hebrew chereb (H2719) — sword, cutting tool; Exodus 20:25, Deuteronomy 27:5, thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them.
Hebrew cheret (H2747) — graving tool, stylus; Exodus 32:4, Isaiah 8:1.
usage: “If thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it” — the altar excluded from improvement.
“Neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house” — a silent temple.
“Fashioned it with a graving tool” — the calf, made by skill alone.

pos: n. pl. (burning lights; rendering Hebrew lappid, Greek lampas)
etymology: From Latin torqua, a twist of tow dipped in pitch. A torch is portable fire — light that goes where it is carried.
biblical_def: Torches are carried lights. Gideon's three hundred hide theirs in empty pitchers and break them at midnight, crying, “The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon” (Jdg 7:16,20). Samson ties torches between foxes' tails to burn Philistine corn (Jdg 15:4). And the band that arrests Christ comes to a garden at night “with lanterns and torches and weapons” (Joh 18:3) — carrying fire to seize the Light of the world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines torch as a light or luminary formed of some combustible substance, as of resinous wood, or of flax or hemp dipped in tallow.
webster_full: TORCH, n. A light or luminary formed of some combustible substance, as of resinous wood, or of flax or hemp dipped in tallow or other inflammable liquor.
scriptures: Jdg 7:16
And he divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers. a
Jdg 7:20

And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon.
Joh 18:3
Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.
Jdg 15:4
And Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails.
corruption_summary: Strength is sought in numbers and equipment, and Gideon's army was reduced to three hundred men holding trumpets, empty jars, and light.
corruption_paragraphs: Gideon's battle plan required that the light stay hidden until the jars were broken. Three hundred men surrounded a camp, each with a trumpet in one hand and a torch concealed in an earthen pitcher in the other — which meant no hand was left for a sword. The victory came at the moment the vessels shattered and the light came out. Paul's line about treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God and not of us, is the same picture with the theology stated.
roots_summary: Hebrew lappid (H3940), a torch or flame; Greek lampas (G2985), a torch or lamp — the word for the virgins' lamps in Matthew 25.
roots_lines: Hebrew lappid (H3940) — torch, firebrand; Judges 7:16, 15:4, Genesis 15:17, a burning lamp between the pieces.
Greek lampas (G2985) — torch, lamp; John 18:3, Matthew 25:1-8.
usage: “Lamps within the pitchers” — light hidden until the vessels broke.
“The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon” — no hand left for a sword.
“With lanterns and torches and weapons” — fire carried to arrest the Light.

etymology: From Dutch wagen. In Genesis the wagons are evidence — the thing that finally persuaded an old man his son was alive.
biblical_def: Wagons are wheeled carts. Pharaoh sends them to carry Jacob's household to Egypt, and they become the proof that convinces him: “when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father revived” (Gen 45:27). The princes bring six covered wagons for the Levites' service of the tabernacle (Num 7:3), and Ezekiel warns of enemies coming “with chariots, wagons, and wheels” (Eze 23:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wagon as a vehicle moved on wheels, and usually drawn by horses or oxen, used for the transportation of heavy commodities.
webster_full: WAGON, n. A vehicle moved on wheels, and usually drawn by horses or oxen; used for the transportation of heavy commodities.
scriptures: And they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said unto them: and when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father revived:
Now thou art commanded, this do ye; take you wagons out of the land of Egypt for your little ones, and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.
Num 7:3
And they brought their offering before the LORD, six covered wagons, and twelve oxen; a wagon for two of the princes, and for each one an ox: and they brought them before the tabernacle.
And told him, saying, Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt. And Jacob's heart fainted, for he believed them not. Jacob's: Heb. his
corruption_summary: Good news that is too good is disbelieved first and evidenced second, and Jacob needed to see the wagons before his heart could accept what his ears had heard.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 45:26 records the first response: Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt. And Jacob's heart fainted, for he believed them not. The report was true, delivered by eyewitnesses who were his own sons, and it was too large to receive. Then he saw the wagons — ordinary carts, sent by a living man with authority to send them — and the spirit of Jacob their father revived. God frequently attaches something visible to a promise too big to hold, not because the word was insufficient but because the hearer was.
roots_summary: Hebrew agalah (H5699), a cart or wagon — also the new cart on which the ark was wrongly carried in 2 Samuel 6.
roots_lines: Hebrew agalah (H5699) — cart, wagon; Genesis 45:19-27, Numbers 7:3-8, 1 Samuel 6:7.
Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, revive; Genesis 45:27, the spirit of Jacob revived.
usage: “When he saw the wagons… the spirit of Jacob their father revived” — evidence for a heart that fainted.
“Take you wagons out of the land of Egypt” — Pharaoh's provision.
“Six covered wagons, and twelve oxen” — for the Levites' burden.

pos: n. (woven work; also a spider's snare; rendering Hebrew massaketh and qur)
etymology: Old English webb, from weave. Scripture uses the word for cloth on a loom and for the spider's fragile trap.
biblical_def: A web is woven work. Delilah weaves the seven locks of Samson's head “with the web” on a loom (Jdg 16:13). Job makes it an image of the hypocrite's confidence: “whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web” (Job 8:14). Isaiah says of the wicked, “they weave the spider's web… their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works” (Isa 59:5–6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines web as texture of threads; any thing woven; and the fine texture spun by a spider.
webster_full: WEB, n. Texture of threads; any thing woven.
2. A whole piece of linen cloth as it is woven.
3. The fine texture which a spider spins for catching flies.
scriptures: Job 8:14
Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web.
Isa 59:5
They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the spider's web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth, and that which is crushed breaketh out into a viper.
Isa 59:6
Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works: their works are works of iniquity, and the act of violence is in their hands.
And Delilah said unto Samson, Hitherto thou hast mocked me, and told me lies: tell me wherewith thou mightest be bound. And he said unto her, If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web.
corruption_summary: Self-made righteousness is not condemned for being ugly but for being insufficient — Isaiah says the webs simply will not cover anyone.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's image is precise about the failure. A spider's web is genuinely woven, genuinely intricate, and genuinely the creature's own work — and it will not serve as clothing. Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works. The problem with self-righteousness is not that it involves no effort but that the material cannot do the job required of it. Only two chapters later Isaiah names the alternative: he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness.
roots_summary: Hebrew massaketh (H4545), a web on a loom; qur (H6980), a spider's thread; akkabish (H5908), spider.
roots_lines: Hebrew massaketh (H4545) — web, warp on a loom; only Judges 16:13-14.
Hebrew qur (H6980) — spider's thread, web; Isaiah 59:5-6, Job 8:14.
usage: “Whose trust shall be a spider's web” — real work, fatal material.
“Their webs shall not become garments” — self-righteousness will not cover.
“If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web” — Samson at the loom.

pos: n. (a bar of metal; rendering Hebrew lashon, a tongue)
etymology: Old English wecg. The Hebrew calls it a tongue of gold — a cast bar shaped like one, and in Achan's case a tongue that testified against him.
biblical_def: A wedge is a cast bar of metal. Achan confesses his: “a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight… and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent” (Jos 7:21). Isaiah promises scarcity: “I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir” (Isa 13:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wedge as a mass of metal, particularly of gold or silver; and a piece of metal, thick at one end and sloping to a thin edge at the other, used in splitting wood.
webster_full: WEDGE, n. A mass of metal, particularly of gold or silver.
2. A piece of metal, thick at one end and sloping to a thin edge at the other, used in splitting wood, rocks, etc.
scriptures: Jos 7:21

When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it.
I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir.
Jos 7:24

And Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver, and the garment, and the wedge of gold, and his sons, and his daughters, and his oxen, and his asses, and his sheep, and his tent, and all that he had: and they brought them unto the valley of Achor.
Jos 7:11

Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff.
corruption_summary: Private sin is assumed to be private, and Joshua 7 opens with the whole nation defeated because one man had something buried under his tent floor.
corruption_paragraphs: Achan's confession follows a sequence he probably did not notice at the time: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. Nothing in it was public, and the plunder was buried under the floor of his own tent. Yet Joshua 7 opens with the words the children of Israel committed a trespass — plural — and thirty-six men died at Ai before anyone knew why. Covenant community means a buried wedge of gold is never as private as its owner believes.
roots_summary: Hebrew lashon (H3956), tongue — used of a cast bar of gold in Joshua 7:21; ketem (H3800), pure gold, in Isaiah 13:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew lashon (H3956) — tongue, wedge; Joshua 7:21, 24, literally a tongue of gold.
Hebrew ketem (H3800) — fine gold; Isaiah 13:12, the golden wedge of Ophir.
usage: “A wedge of gold… hid in the earth in the midst of my tent” — buried and not private.
“I saw… I coveted… I took… I hid” — the sequence Achan names.
“A man more precious than… the golden wedge of Ophir” — scarcity in judgment.

etymology: Old English gearn. Yarn appears in Scripture in a single commercial note about Solomon's imports — and the trade it names is itself a warning.
biblical_def: Yarn is spun thread. It occurs in the record of Solomon's horse trade: “Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price” (1Ki 10:28; 2Ch 1:16). The detail matters because the same king had been given a law forbidding exactly this: “he shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt” (Deu 17:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yarn as thread spun; the thread of tow, hemp, flax, wool or cotton, spun on a wheel; and one of the threads of which a rope is composed.
webster_full: YARN, n. Thread; spun wool; woolen thread.
2. Thread of tow, hemp, flax, or cotton.
3. One of the threads of which a rope is composed.
scriptures: And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price. And
And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price.

But he shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt, to the end that he should multiply horses: forasmuch as the LORD hath said unto you, Ye shall henceforth return no more that way.
For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.
corruption_summary: Decline is recorded in inventory rather than in scandal, and Solomon's fall is visible first in a shipping manifest that violated a law he knew.
corruption_paragraphs: The chronicler's note about horses and linen yarn reads as prosperity and is in fact an indictment. Deuteronomy 17 had set three limits for a king — not many horses, not many wives, not much silver and gold — and required him to write out a copy of the law himself. Solomon breached all three, and the record of it sits in the middle of the chapters describing his glory. Compromise rarely announces itself; it shows up in a procurement decision that everyone approves of at the time.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqveh (H4723), a collection or drove — rendered linen yarn by the KJV, read by some as a place-name; the trade route is Egypt.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqveh (H4723) — gathering, drove, linen yarn; 1 Kings 10:28, 2 Chronicles 1:16.
Hebrew sus (H5483) — horse; the commodity Deuteronomy 17:16 forbade multiplying.
usage: “Horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn” — prosperity that broke a command.
“The king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price” — the trade formalized.
“He shall not multiply horses… nor cause the people to return to Egypt” — the law he knew.
